OrthoRef · Shoulder girdle · Rockwood & Green 10e, Ch. 34

Clavicle Fractures

Midshaft, lateral and medial fractures — assessment, classification, the operative-versus-sling decision, fixation technique and complications.

Sources: Woltz & McKee, Rockwood and Green’s Fractures in Adults 10e, Ch. 34 · AO Foundation Surgery Reference (marked AO)

OverviewClavicle fractures at a glance

Common, usually midshaft, and mostly best treated in a sling — yet displaced fractures carry a real nonunion and malunion burden, so a selected subset benefits from fixation after shared decision-making.

2.6–4%of all fractures
29–64per 100,000 per year
80–85%midshaft
15–20%distal third
0–5%medial third
Who

Young men, then a second peak

Males predominate in every age group up to ~60, peaking under 25; newer data show a smaller second peak in middle-aged men. Females peak as teenagers and in the elderly (osteoporotic falls).

Where

Midshaft: thinnest, curved, unprotected

The middle portion is narrowest and lacks the muscular and ligamentous cover of either end — combined with compressive shoulder loading, it fails most often.

How

Direct blow to the point of the shoulder

Most common mechanism, ahead of a fall on the outstretched hand. The classic scenario is a bicycle fall — predominant in 25–65-year-olds where cycling is popular.

Principle

Operative treatment has a relatively narrow risk–benefit ratio: complications are common, long-term shoulder function is often similar, and the majority of clavicle fractures can — and should — be treated nonoperatively.

How the paradigm shifted — a timeline
30th century BC

Edwin Smith papyrus records the earliest closed reduction of a displaced midshaft fracture.

400 BC

Hippocrates counsels essentially benign neglect: the fracture unites quickly even if physicians “cannot make the parts look well.”

1960 · 1968

Neer (3 nonunions in 2,235) and Rowe (4 in 566) report virtually no nonunion with sling or figure-of-eight; malunion deemed of radiographic interest only.

~2000 onward

Studies excluding children and nondisplaced fractures, with patient-reported outcomes, show true nonunion of 10–15% and frequent residual pain; malunion emerges as a clinical entity.

2007

Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society publishes the first RCT: plate fixation lowered nonunion and improved arm function versus nonoperative care.

2001–2012

Sweden: clavicle fracture incidence rose 67% (36 → 59 per 100,000) while surgical fixation rose 705%.

History · examination · imagingAssessment

History — the mechanism tells you what else to look for

  • Simple low-energy fall → associated fractures or intrathoracic injury unlikely.
  • Severe vehicular trauma or fall from height → search for other injuries.
  • Traction mechanism (arm pulled from the body in machinery, or pinned while the torso continues) → scapulothoracic dissociation: a distracted rather than overlapping fracture; high rate of neurovascular traction injury, investigate with angiography — potentially limb-threatening.
  • Minimal trauma → consider pathologic fracture (renal disease, hyperparathyroidism, myeloma, metastases, congenital pseudarthrosis). Treat the clavicle nonoperatively initially while the underlying condition is diagnosed.
  • Repetitive/unusual loading → stress fracture (bodybuilders, weightlifters).
  • Take a social and occupational history: compliance, overhead or lifting work, sport, and patient preferences all feed the operative decision.

Examination

Inspect standing

Shoulder “ptosis”

Droopy, medially driven, shortened shoulder that translates and rotates forward; from behind, the inferior scapula may be prominent from protraction.

Skin

Tenting = urgent

Skin compromised by a displaced fragment warrants prompt reduction and fixation to prevent a secondary open fracture.

Measure

Tape-measure shortening

Suprasternal notch midline to the palpable AC ridge, compared side-to-side. Shortening beyond 1.5–2 cm carries a worse prognosis.

Pitfalls
  • Radiographs — especially of long oblique fractures — tend to overestimate shortening; clinical measurement matters.
  • About 30% of people have physiologic asymmetry between clavicles (mean 5 mm difference).
  • A careful neurovascular examination is mandatory before surgery; an undocumented pre-existing deficit may be wrongly attributed to the operation.

Open fractures

  • Rare given the subcutaneous position; usually high-energy, with a high rate of associated injury.
  • Taitsman (20 patients): 15 pulmonary and 13 head injuries.
  • Gottschalk (53 over 16 years, ~3/year): penetrating injuries → great-vessel injury; blunt injuries → 52% serious head injury.
  • Give prophylactic antibiotics; instability generally warrants operative stabilization as soon as the patient’s condition allows.

Imaging

RegionFirst-lineKey points
MidshaftUpright AP + 15–40° cephalic tiltIf only one film, choose the tilted view. Chest film compares length with the other side — ≥2 cm shortening is a relative indication for fixation. Consider repeat films at 1 week (early progressive displacement from muscle pull). CT not routine.
PolytraumaSupine trauma chest filmUnderestimates displacement: Backus found 89% more displacement on upright films (46 patients), enough to change management. Repeat upright two-view clavicle films once the patient allows.
Lateral thirdZanca: ~15° cephalic, centred on AC jointStanding, arm unsupported. Plain films can underestimate posterior displacement — correlate clinically. Stress view with 2.26–4.53 kg (5–10 lb) hung from the wrist tests CC integrity. CT rarely needed (intra-articular extension).
Medial thirdCTPlain films notoriously poor. CT distinguishes a medial physeal fracture (common up to age 25) from a true SC dislocation.

PolytraumaAssociated injuries

80%associated injuries in polytrauma (ISS ≥16)
20–34%mortality — chest & head
55–65%midshaft share in polytrauma
60% vs 29%rib fractures with vs without a clavicle fracture
<1%subclavian / plexus injury
  • Head and neck, and thoracic cage: ipsilateral rib, scapular/glenoid and proximal humeral fractures, haemo/pneumothorax.
  • A clavicle fracture on the primary-survey chest film should raise suspicion for other injuries.
  • Associated injuries may need their own urgent treatment (e.g. chest drain) or change clavicle management — multiple upper rib fractures or a displaced glenoid neck fracture (“floating shoulder”) may favour fixation.
  • Medial fractures are usually high-energy: associated injuries in up to 80% and ~20% mortality — CT is advised.
  • Local neurovascular injury (subclavian/axillary vessels, brachial plexus) is rare (<1%) and warrants CT angiography or MRI.
Outcome measures — why “united” is not the same as “recovered”
  • Gossard: 15% of nonoperatively treated patients were dissatisfied despite radiographic union.
  • Woltz: despite union and excellent scores, half of patients perceived incomplete recovery years later (after both operative and nonoperative care).
  • McKee: machine-measured strength deficits up to 30% after malunion, missed on manual testing.
  • Typical battery: general health (SF-36/MFA), limb-specific (DASH/ASES), surgeon-based (Constant/UCLA) and radiographic measures.
  • DASH and Constant have a ceiling effect in this young, fit population — insensitive to minor residual symptoms.
  • Schemitsch: DASH and Constant scores do not change appreciably after 1 year — functional outcome at 1 year is essentially final.

Applied anatomyThe strut of the shoulder girdle

The clavicle is the only true bony connection between the torso and the arm — when it fails, the scapula follows the distal fragment, and that malposition drives much of the late morbidity.

5–6 wkgestation: first bone to ossify
~27 yrlast to complete ossification
<1 cmsubclavian vein from posterior cortex, medial half
≤2 cmartery & vein, middle third
≥45 mmvessels laterally

Bony anatomy

Shape

S-curve in the coronal plane

Medial end convex anteriorly, lateral end concave anteriorly. Smaller clavicles are more curved; larger ones longer and straighter.

Shape

A subtle superior bow

Apex a mean 37 mm from the acromial end, magnitude ~5 mm; the medial superior surface is flat (Huang).

Implants

“Anatomic” plates still need bending

Plate fit varied significantly by sex and race; shape models need 10 modes of variation to explain 95% of shape — expect to adjust precontoured plates.

Cross-section

Flat → tubular → prismatic AO

Lateral to medial the section changes from flat to tubular to prismatic; the flat–tubular junction is a stress riser, explaining midshaft predominance.

Medial · lateralLigaments

Medial (SC joint)

  • Little motion, thick soft tissue. The posterior capsular thickening is the single most important restraint to anterior or posterior translation of the medial clavicle.
  • Interclavicular ligament: runs between the medial ends across the sternal notch, acting as a tension wire against inferior angulation/translation.
  • Costoclavicular ligaments: very stout, from first rib to the clavicle undersurface (rhomboid fossa); resist translation.

Lateral (CC and AC)

  • Coracoclavicular ligaments: trapezoid (lateral, to the trapezoid ridge) and conoid (medial, to the conoid tubercle) — the primary restraint to superior displacement of the lateral clavicle.
  • Their integrity guides decision-making and implant choice in lateral fractures; an avulsed inferior fragment often carries them — include it in fixation.
  • AC capsule is thickened superiorly and resists AP displacement; repair it with the deep myofascial layer. For a hook plate, make only a small posterolateral capsular defect.

Deforming forcesMuscles and the deformity they create

FragmentDisplacementResponsible force
MedialElevatedUnopposed sternocleidomastoid
DistalInferiorDeltoid and gravity (arm weight)
DistalMedial (shortening)Pectoralis major
DistalAnterior translation + anterior rotationInitial force vector plus muscular/gravitational pull — scapula protracts with it
Muscle attachments in detail
  • Pectoralis major and fascia envelope the medial ~60% anterosuperiorly (origin anteroinferior); deltoid covers the lateral ~40%.
  • Sternocleidomastoid originates superiorly on the medial clavicle; trapezius attaches posterosuperiorly and blends with the deltoid origin laterally.
  • Subclavius inserts on the undersurface — functionally minor, but a soft-tissue buffer above the plexus and subclavian vessels.
  • In the tubular middle third the subclavius muscle and fascia protect the neurovascular structures from the fracture. AO
  • Platysma is divided in the approach and closed with the skin/subcutaneous layer.

What the drill can reachNeurovascular relations

Supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4)

  • Exit from a common trunk behind the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid; typically anterior, middle and posterior branches cross the clavicle.
  • Division → numbness inferior to the incision, usually improving; a vertical incision or nerve-sparing technique lowers risk.
  • Warn patients preoperatively; a painful scar neuroma is rare but troublesome.

Great vessels and plexus

  • Subclavian vein runs directly below subclavius, above the first rib.
  • Subclavian artery and plexus lie more posteriorly, separated medially by scalenus anterior. The plexus is closest to the clavicle in its midportion.
  • Vessels pass posterosuperior → anteroinferior between first rib and clavicle at the junction of the medial and middle thirds. AO
  • Anterior plating could theoretically be safer than superior plating for midshaft fractures — not proven clinically.
Danger zone

The vein lies within 1 cm of the posterior cortex along the entire medial half; take extreme care manipulating medial fragments. Iatrogenic injury is nonetheless surprisingly rare.

Location first, then prognosisClassification

Every scheme starts with which third; the useful ones then add displacement, comminution, articular extension and — laterally — the status of the CC ligaments.

Source note

The R&G chapter text lists the diaphyseal subtypes as 15.2-B1/B2/B3, whereas the reproduced 2018 compendium (Fig. 34-14) labels them 15.2A/B/C. The table follows the figure.

Pearl

Distal fractures are entrenched in the lexicon as “Type II” (Neer) — but in Robinson’s scheme lateral fractures are Type 3. Say which system you mean.

Treatment optionsMidshaft fractures

Randomized trials agree: fixation of displaced midshaft fractures lowers nonunion and symptomatic malunion and speeds early recovery — but it adds implant problems and rarely beats sling treatment on long-term function.

Nonoperative treatment

Device

A simple sling

Padded neckpiece, no attempt at reduction. No device (figure-of-eight, casts, braces) reliably maintains reduction or improves outcome.

Figure-of-eight

No better, more trouble

No functional/radiographic advantage over a sling; more dissatisfaction, more day-1 pain (VAS 6.8 vs 5.6), and overtightening can cause lower-trunk plexus palsy.

Rehab

Sling 1–2 weeks

Pendulums, then active non-weight-bearing motion up to horizontal. Radiographs at 6 weeks; strengthen thereafter if no delayed union.

Outcomes after nonoperative care of displaced midshaft fractures
  • Nonunion 14–24% in reviews; 13.8% (78/567) in a meta-analysis of 24 RCTs; 21% for displaced comminuted fractures (Robinson, 868 patients).
  • Nowak: at 10 years 46% still had symptoms although only 7% had a nonunion.
  • Woltz: 41% residual symptoms and 54% perceived incomplete recovery at 4 years.
  • Scores are still good overall: DASH ~2–12 and Constant ~80–98 at 1 year; differences from surgery usually fall below the MCID. Analyses of united fractures only show equivalent function.
  • Cosmesis: patients are less satisfied after nonoperative care — COTS 52/62 operative vs 26/49 nonoperative satisfied with appearance; another study 8.2 vs 6.8/10. Many assume the bump will remodel — counsel early.

* More absolute indications; the rest are relative.

Contra-indications
  • Drug or alcohol abuse, untreated psychiatric illness, homelessness, uncontrolled seizures — noncompliance drives fixation failure.
  • No clavicular fixation withstands an unprotected fall downstairs or a fight in the early postoperative period.
Displaced =

>1 shaft width, >1.5–2 cm shortening

…plus associated rotational deformity or scapular winging (Algorithm 34-1 definition).

High demand

<60, >16, active, healthy

→ shared decision-making → operative fixation with a precontoured plate or an intramedullary pin.

Low demand

>60, <16, comorbid, substance abuse

→ nonoperative: sling, range of motion when comfortable. Undisplaced fractures go the same way.

Tipping the scale

  • Multiple risk factors for failed nonoperative care (e.g. female sex plus unfavourable fracture characteristics) can favour surgery.
  • Nonunion probability worsens with increasing age, comminution, displacement and female sex (prognostic index, Fig. 34-20).
  • Healthy, active patients over 60 can still be considered for fixation.
  • Adolescents: a prospective study of 416 showed no benefit of surgery for function, union or complications — reserve for older, larger adolescents with severe displacement or shortening.

Timing

  • Preferably within 2–3 weeks; difficulty of reduction does not rise until ~2 weeks, so waiting for bruised skin to settle is reasonable.
  • Das: early (<3 weeks, n=68) vs delayed (3–12 weeks, n=29) plating — no difference in soft-tissue complications, union, hardware removal or outcomes.
  • But “wait and see” forfeits the early-function advantage, and Jeyaseelan reported 21 iatrogenic plexus injuries — mean 3 weeks to fixation — with the upper trunk/C5–C6 tethered to the clavicle undersurface.
  • Closed IM reduction is usually only achievable in about the first week.
Delayed fixation

If fixing late, carefully dissect adherent soft tissue off the inferior clavicle during reduction.

Choosing the implant

OptionStrengthsLimitations / evidence
Plate (precontoured)Gold standard: union 94–100%; nonunion 2.2% (460) and 1.3% (899) in meta-analysesImplant irritation and removal; reoperation for adverse events (excluding removal) ~2–7%
Unlocked elastic nail (ESIN/TEN)Small cosmetic incision, less stripping, easy removalNo control of length/rotation; migration and breakage; van der Meijden (120): plate had less early disability and TEN removal was advised for all; slower recovery in comminuted fractures (Fuglesang)
Threaded pins (Hagie/Rockwood)Threaded medial end, lateral compression nutRotation and length still hard to hold; plates superior in biomechanical testing (Golish)
Locked IM nailHolds length; lower migration and removalBetter function vs plates in one meta-analysis (895) was attributable solely to locked nails; more data needed for unstable patterns
External fixationNo retained hardware; useful with badly compromised soft tissuePin position/prominence and poor patient acceptance — minimal use
Rule of thumb

Unlocked IM devices suit simple transverse and short oblique fractures with an accommodating canal, with removal expected after healing; comminuted and unstable patterns belong to a plate.

Plate vs sling — the trial evidence
  • Clavicle Trial (Ahrens, >300 patients): nonunion 11% sling vs 1% plate at 9 months, better early function with plating.
  • Woltz (160 randomized): nonunion 23% nonoperative vs 2% plate; 9 of 16 nonunions needed surgery. More reinterventions (mostly removal) after plating; function similar. At 4.3 years, 55% of plated patients still had symptoms and 53% reported incomplete recovery.
  • Melean: faster return to work with plating in workers’ compensation claimants.
  • Functional gains rarely exceed the MCID (8 Constant, 10 DASH); the advantage is mostly seen around 6 weeks.
  • Conclusion: plate fixation for a selected subgroup with completely displaced fractures — union ~95%, low complication rate — decided with the patient.
Postoperative care after plating
  • Usually outpatient. Sling for comfort, gentle pendulums; wound check at 10–14 days.
  • Discard the sling as pain allows; unrestricted range of motion but no strengthening, resisted exercise or sport.
  • Radiographs at 6 weeks → start resisted and strengthening work. Avoid contact or unpredictable sports for 12 weeks.
  • Routine implant removal after union is not recommended.

Treatment optionsLateral (distal) fractures

Displaced distal fractures have a high nonunion rate, yet most nonunions are well tolerated — nonoperative care is acceptable in most, with fixation for fully displaced, unstable fractures in high-demand patients or failed nonoperative care.

20–36%nonunion after nonoperative care of displaced fractures
9–47%of those nonunions ever operated
96–100%union after fixation
60–83%hook plate removal
Evidence for nonoperative care
  • Same regimen as midshaft: sling 2 weeks, pendulums and non-weight-bearing motion to horizontal, radiographs and progression at 6 weeks.
  • Raval (UK, 275 Neer II): 72% treated nonoperatively; 33% nonunion, but only 4/43 (9%) had surgery.
  • Srinivasan: only 22% of nonunions underwent secondary fixation.
  • van der Linde (619 patients, mean 7 years): displaced nonoperative fractures — 20% nonunion, about half operated; DASH 7.8, high satisfaction, 97% back to work; comparable to surgery.
  • Hall RCT (57 patients): 36% nonunion nonoperatively but no difference in arm function; 20% had secondary surgery and return to activity took longer.
Preferred

Precontoured locking plate

Lateral extension for multiple 2.7-mm locking screws. The authors add a suture button only when distal purchase is inadequate.

Augment

CC suture button

Through a plate hole into the coracoid base; most cost-effective option (Fox), low revision rates, but coracoid fracture is a specific complication.

Alternative

Hook plate

Reliable purchase under the acromion; Elrih meta-analysis (523): locking plate had similar function and fewer complications/reoperations. Advise against routine use.

Failure mode

Distal fixation fails by pull-out of the distal fragment with redisplacement of the shaft AO. Expect unrecognized comminution and weaker cancellous bone distally — have a hook plate or CC device ready.

Other injuriesMedial fractures, floating shoulder and rib injuries

Medial fractures

  • Often physeal injuries in the young — the medial clavicular physis can persist to 25–30 years; CT defines fracture-subluxation vs dislocation.
  • 60–80% undisplaced → nonoperative; nonunion 0–4.6%.
  • Significant displacement — especially posterior displacement of the shaft — may warrant fixation.
  • The medial expansion allows longer screws (often 25–30 mm); an inverted distal clavicle plate can increase purchase.
  • Poor medial purchase: extend the plate onto the sternum and remove it at ~3 months after union. Smooth wires/pins alone are contraindicated (migration).

“Floating shoulder”

  • Ipsilateral clavicle + scapular (glenoid) neck fractures — the commonest double disruption of the superior shoulder suspensory complex.
  • Clavicle fixation alone often indirectly reduces and stabilizes the glenoid.
  • Fix the clavicle first, re-image; if glenoid alignment remains unacceptable, fix it through a posterior approach.
  • Oh reported failures of isolated clavicle fixation — use an implant sized for the higher loads.

Associated rib fractures

  • Stahl: ipsilateral rib fractures, especially upper third, significantly increase clavicle displacement — an unstable injury that tends to progress.
  • Onizuka: rib fractures are a risk factor for progressive displacement in weeks 1–3.
  • Follow these patients closely; severe chest-wall instability is a relative indication for clavicle fixation.

Midshaft fixationPlate position

Two plate positions dominate — anterosuperior (most popular) and anteroinferior. Union, plate failure and function are the same clinically; they differ in screw trajectory, prominence and removal.

AnterosuperiorAnteroinferior
FamiliarityMost surgeons; extends easily medially and laterallyLess familiar
Screw trajectorySuperior → inferior toward lung and NV structures — “plunging” riskEasier, safer trajectory
Screw lengthNarrow superoinferiorly: ~14–16 mm (women), 16–18 mm (men)Longer screws in the wider AP dimension
ImagingClear postoperative radiographsPlate obscures the fracture
BiomechanicsStiffer/stronger in bending for transverse fracturesStability lost with comminution in either position
Removal (meta-analysis)11%5% (p = .008), less prominence
Dual mini-fragment plating
  • 2017 series: high union, 2/81 implant removals, but longer surgery and more dissection.
  • Rompen meta-analysis: union similar to single 3.5-mm plating, fewer complications and reinterventions (less irritation).
  • More high-quality comparative data needed; newer single 2.7-mm precontoured plates may make dual plating unnecessary.

ExposureSurgical approach

Setup (R&G)

  • Beach-chair/semisitting on a regular OR table or shoulder table; head on a round support, ET tube taped to the opposite side.
  • Arm padded and strapped to the side for isolated injuries; small pad behind the involved shoulder — check the superior drill path is unobstructed.
  • Fluoroscopy optional for midshaft plating.

Exposure (R&G)

  • Oblique incision centred superiorly over the fracture (or vertical).
  • Keep subcutaneous tissue + platysma as one layer, mobilized widely; protect larger supraclavicular branches.
  • Incise and elevate the myofascial layer as one continuous sheet → two layers to close over the plate.
  • Preserve soft-tissue attachments to every major fragment.
Anterior approach · AO

For nearly any shaft fracture

Usable for anterior or superior plating. Incise and tag the platysma, identify and preserve supraclavicular nerves, incise the clavipectoral fascia (pectoralis major anterior, trapezius posterior) with minimal dissection; close the clavipectoral fascia over the plate.

Superior approach · AO

Lateral fractures, superior plates

Deltoid reflected from the lateral clavicle anteriorly and posteriorly in a contiguous sheet. Accept some malreduction rather than strip comminuted fragments; re-appose the platysma exactly to avoid skin deformity.

WalkthroughPlate fixation — key steps

Step walkthrough · midshaft plate fixation
STEP 1 / 5

Read the fracture

Before plating, study the pattern: a size mismatch between fragment ends at the fracture implies rotation; look for the vertically oriented anterosuperior fragment and count how many screws the distal fragment will take — choose plate length (or a lateral plate) accordingly.

STEP 2 / 5

Lag the wedge to its parent

A free fragment of about one-third of the circumference or more is structurally important: preserve its soft-tissue hinge, reduce it to the fragment it came from and lag it (e.g. countersunk 2.7-mm), converting the fracture to a simple pattern.

STEP 3 / 5

Tease the Z-pattern home

Reduce the vertical intercalary fragment to the distal fragment and secure it, then reduce the distal assembly to the proximal fragment with two towel-clip forceps; hold with a K-wire or, ideally, a second lag screw. Never denude the fragment.

STEP 4 / 5

Choose a plate strong enough

With a lag screw: 3 bicortical screws (6 cortices) each side. Without one: 4 screws each side or a locking plate. Compression mode for stable patterns, neutral for comminution. Avoid 3.5-mm reconstruction plates — this one deformed in a >200-lb patient.

STEP 5 / 5

Never rely on cerclage alone

Isolated cerclage wiring cannot control the deforming forces — all the risks of surgery with few of the benefits. Finish with a two-layer absorbable closure; if pleural breach is suspected, fill with saline and ask for a Valsalva.

Screws

Nonlocking screws are usually sufficient in young, good-quality bone; use locking or variable-angle locking holes in poorer bone or when the plate cannot sit perfectly central.

TechniqueIntramedullary pinning

  • Radiolucent or shoulder table, semisitting with a small pad between the scapulae (lets the shoulder fall back and aids reduction).
  • C-arm contralateral (or ipsilateral/cranial); rotate 45° caudal and 45° cephalad for orthogonal views. Visualize the whole clavicle before draping.
  • Retrograde: small incision over the posterolateral corner 2–3 cm medial to the AC joint; antegrade: anteromedial entry.
  • Open the canal, pass through the near fragment, reduce (percutaneous clamp + joystick, or small open incision) and seat in the far fragment; ream if the device requires.
  • Alternative “inside-out”: pass out through the lateral fragment from the fracture, reduce, then drive medially.
  • Do not distract: the straight pin meets the far cortex of the S-shaped bone — withdraw slightly or use a shorter pin.
  • Leave the head prominent for early removal (7–8 weeks) or flush to reduce irritation. Sling, wound check at 2 weeks, radiographs and strengthening at 6 weeks.
IM pinning — pitfalls and preventions
PitfallPrevention
Inadequate visualizationImage the entire clavicle before prepping
Cannot pass the pinSelect patients with a canal large enough for the device
Iatrogenic comminutionAppropriate canal size; hold reduction while crossing; don’t joystick with the device
Neurovascular injuryAvoid extraosseous posterior/inferior passage of instruments
Early hardware failureMatch device to size, fracture and compliance
Malunion / shorteningAvoid IM fixation in comminuted fractures
High removal rateChoose a locked device

TechniqueLateral clavicle fixation

  • Radiolucent/shoulder table — fluoroscopy is essential to confirm distal screws are out of the AC joint.
  • Incision directly superior over the distal clavicle, ~1 cm past the AC joint; reflect the deltotrapezial layer; locate the joint with an 18-G needle (avoid arthrotomy).
  • Reduce (elevating the distal fragment helps), hold with a K-wire; apply a precontoured lateral plate with multiple 2.7-mm locking screws distally.
  • At least 3 bicortical screws in the shaft fragment; preserve the AC capsule — it stabilizes the small distal fragment. AO
  • If distal fixation is inadequate: add a CC suture button through a plate hole, or convert to a hook plate. A rigid CC screw loosens or breaks — no longer advised.

Suture button

  • Tilt the C-arm ~15° ipsilaterally from AP until the coracoid appears as a circle.
  • K-wire into the middle of the coracoid base → cannulated drill → pass device; tightening it can itself reduce the fracture when planned from the start.
  • Deltoid split for direct coracoid vision is usually unnecessary.

Hook plate

  • Free the posterior edge of the distal clavicle; open a path into the subacromial space posteriorly with heavy curved scissors — avoid the tight anterior space (cuff impingement).
  • Trial hook depths/lengths, or “walk” the plate down distal-to-proximal.
  • Needing heavy contouring usually means the fracture is not reduced; check for over-reduction on imaging.
  • Plan removal (commonly ≥6 months) to restore terminal flexion/abduction.
Lateral fixation — pitfalls, prevention and aftercare
PitfallPrevention
Loss of distal fixationPrecontoured plate with multiple distal locking screws; hook plate or suture-button augmentation if bone inadequate
Over-reduction (hook plate)Correct hook depth/angle; confirm on imaging
Intra-articular AC screwsVisual and radiographic check before closure
Deep infectionTwo-layer closure
Delayed/nonunionAvoid excessive stripping
Hardware irritationPrecontoured distal plate, suture button instead of hook plate, or newer low-profile hook design
  • Aftercare: sling and pendulums; wound check at 10–14 days then discard the sling (longer if fixation doubtful); resistance at 6–8 weeks; contact sports after 12 weeks.

Prevention and treatmentComplications

Nonoperative care trades on nonunion and malunion; operative care trades on infection, hardware and neurovascular risk. Know both ledgers.

ComplicationPreventionTreatment
InfectionCareful technique, short operative time, prophylactic antibioticsSuperficial: oral antibiotics. Deep: I&D, IV antibiotics, keep fixation if stable, remove if loose
NonunionPrimary fixation in selected casesDebride, plate ± lag screw; iliac crest graft or osteoinductive substitute if atrophic
MalunionPrimary fixation in selected casesCorrective osteotomy and plate fixation
Neurovascular injuryCareful techniqueUsually expectant; prevention is key
Hardware failurePlate strong enough for patient; avoid 3.5-mm reconstruction platesObserve if not badly displaced; otherwise revise with a stronger plate. Late failure = delayed/nonunion
Hardware prominencePrecontoured plate, especially in smaller patientsRemoval after at least 1–2 years
RefractureAvoid plate removal for 1–2 yearsMinimally displaced → nonoperative; displaced/unstable → repeat ORIF
Scapular wingingPrimary fixation reduces incidence (due to malunion/nonunion)Corrective clavicle surgery if severe

Infection

2–4%deep infection after fixation
≥4deep cultures at debridement

Stable implant

  • DAIR: debridement, antibiotics, implant retention.
  • Withhold antibiotics until cultures are taken; tailor systemic therapy to results, sometimes until union — then remove the plate.
  • Sometimes temporize with wound care and antibiotics until union, then remove, debride and irrigate.

Unstable implant

  • If bone is progressing toward union, temporize then remove.
  • Otherwise: remove hardware, radically debride, irrigate.
  • Healthy host + sensitive organism → immediate replating, grafting and local antibiotics (e.g. vancomycin powder).
  • Polymicrobial/resistant (MRSA) → antibiotic beads or antibiotic-loaded substitute, staged reconstruction.
  • Soft-tissue deficit → plastic surgery, typically a rotational pectoralis major flap.

Defined as no radiographic healing at 6–9 monthsNonunion

Fracture-related risk factorPatient-related risk factor
Complete displacement (most studies)Female sex
ComminutionOlder age
Shortening >2 cmSmoking
DASH >35 at 6 weeks
Minimal pain decrease between weeks 2 and 4
Clement

Smoking + DASH ≥35 at 6 weeks

No risk factor: 2% symptomatic nonunion; both: 44%.

Qvist

Pain that does not settle

Minimal pain improvement between 2 and 4 weeks → twice the risk of symptomatic nonunion.

Leroux

After primary fixation (1,350)

Female sex (OR 2.2) and high comorbidity (OR 2.8) predicted nonunion.

Authors’ preferred repair

  • Precontoured anatomic plate, usually without iliac crest graft.
  • Bring the distal fragment out to length, translate it superiorly and posteriorly, derotate so the flat surface faces up.
  • Rongeur sclerotic ends to bleeding bone; re-open canals with a drill; save and morcellize excess callus as graft.
  • Lag screw if the nonunion line allows; ≥3 bicortical screws each side is the absolute minimum; compress transverse nonunions.
  • If more biology is needed: iliac crest autograft or an osteoinductive substitute (e.g. BMP). Avoid calcium phosphate/sulfate, allograft and DBM.
  • Large bone loss: intercalary graft (Jupiter and Ring). Claviculectomy is a last-resort salvage with strength loss.

Key facts

  • About two-thirds of nonunions are symptomatic enough for surgery; distal nonunions in the elderly are often asymptomatic.
  • Bone graft is often unnecessary if the defect is ≤1.5–2 cm and compression is achieved; Huang found no healing or function difference in atrophic nonunions with or without graft.
  • Short 4-hole, one-third tubular and 3.5-mm reconstruction plates fail.
  • Nonunion after plating: suspect occult infection — C. acnes (Gausden 15/18 cultures positive, 14 C. acnes; another series 11/21).
  • Nicholson: beyond a “safe window” of 96 days, infection (OR 7.7), fixation failure (OR 3.8) and revision (OR 4.8) rise.
  • Late reconstruction scores lower than primary fixation (Potter: Constant 89 vs 95); Fox: QuickDASH 16.5 vs 5.5 vs matched nonoperative unions — yet cost-effective.

A distinct clinical entityMalunion

Orthopaedic

Weakness and fatigability

Shortened muscle–tendon units: loss of maximal and endurance strength, especially abduction.

Neurologic

Thoracic outlet symptoms

Numbness/paraesthesia, usually C8–T1, worse with overhead activity.

“Functional cosmesis”

Straps slide off

Backpacks, military gear and shoulder straps won’t stay; patients dislike the look.

Scapular

Periscapular aching

Malalignment of the scapulothoracic joint — winging, spasm and fatigue pain.

  • Shortening is the predominant risk factor (Eskola: ≥1.2 cm associated with pain), though Woltz’s review of 379 patients found no clear correlation with scores or strength — length is one part of a 3D deformity.
  • Radiographic malunion alone is not an indication; operate for specific, severe symptoms after failed strengthening physiotherapy.
  • Plan length restoration clinically and on a PA chest film including both clavicles (remember 30% asymmetry).

Osteotomy technique

  • Mark bone proximally and distally and measure, to quantify length gained.
  • Recreate the original fracture line with a microsagittal saw and osteotomes, sparing the subclavicular space.
  • Distract carefully — overdistraction risks plexus injury; in long-standing short malunions consider partial correction.
  • Step-cut if possible, re-open canals, K-wire, confirm length, plate, and graft with local morcellized callus. Intercalary graft only for true bone loss.
  • Outcomes: 103 patients in the literature, complication rate 6%, improved scores. 3D-planned guides show promise.

Acute · delayed · iatrogenicNeurovascular injury

Acute

  • Signs of vascular injury → angiography, which can also be therapeutic (embolization, stenting).
  • Most injuries are traction; the extreme is scapulothoracic dissociation with a distracted clavicle — Ebraheim 3/15 deaths; Zelle 3 deaths and 6 amputations in 22.
  • For limb salvage, plate the clavicle to stabilize the girdle.
  • Direct plexus compression by fragments is rare; reduction and fixation are generally advised.

Delayed

  • Thoracic outlet encroachment by displaced fragments or inferior callus → debride callus, realign and fix promptly.
  • Chronic TOS from malunion is the commonest form: treat with corrective clavicular osteotomy — bump excision or first-rib resection fails (McKee: resolution in 16 patients after osteotomy).

Iatrogenic

  • Catastrophic drill/tap injury is very rare; subclavian pseudoaneurysm after nonunion plating has been reported.
  • Ring & Holovacs: 3 plexus palsies after delayed IM fixation from distraction — all recovered. Late correction of a shortened fracture risks traction palsy.
  • Vessel injury (usually during malunion/nonunion surgery): alert the team, pack and compress, call vascular surgery, resuscitate, and lay the patient flat — a subclavian vein defect in the upright position risks air embolism.

Hardware, refracture and scapular winging

Hardware

  • Failure: noncompliance, undersized implant or delayed union. No heavy loading for 6 (preferably 12) weeks.
  • Prominence: precontoured plates reduced removal (Schemitsch, >220 platings); anteroinferior plates 5% vs 11% removal.
  • Leave asymptomatic plates; remove symptomatic ones only after 1–2 years. Unlocked IM devices are usually removed; modern locked nails need not be.

Refracture

  • True refracture is rare — many “refractures” are unhealed original nonunions.
  • Fractures at the end of a plate (high-energy) have a poor natural history: if displaced, refix with a longer plate spanning both sites; if minimally displaced, trial of a sling.
Ristevski · 18 malunions

Acromion follows the fragment

Mean shortening 2.1 cm; acromion translated a mean 2.4 cm medially, inferiorly and anteriorly; superior angle 1 cm, inferior angle 0.6 cm.

Kim · 67 3D CTs

AP-plane shortening matters

Only sagittal (AP) shortening correlated with scapular anterior tilt, internal rotation and upward rotation.

Consequence

Lost mechanical advantage

Rotational strength decreased 13–24% in one study; fatigability and pain may relate to scapular malposition.

Summary

Plating reliably prevents nonunion; sling treatment of displaced fractures carries a 15–20% nonunion rate and persistent malunion. Primary fixation outperforms delayed reconstruction — but functional gains are modest, so select patients carefully and decide together.
